name: heft
summary: Nothing is captured: move onto an enemy piece to shove it, with every piece behind it in that line, one cell on.
A piece shoved off the edge of the board is out. Push out four of the enemy's nine pieces to win.
A shove goes through only if the shover's strength is at least the weight of the whole line it moves.
Bulls step one cell, weigh 3 and shove 4. Darts slide up to two cells, weigh 1 and shove 1. Stones step one cell, weigh 4 and never shove.
Every turn is two moves; the first player's first turn is one.
A piece just shoved may not be shoved straight back on the next move.
If 80 moves pass with nobody pushed out, or the game reaches 300 moves, whoever has more pieces on the seven middle cells wins.
description: A shoving match on a small hexagonal ring. Nothing is ever taken where it stands; a piece is lost only by being shoved over the rim, and a shove is a sum: it moves the whole line in front of the shover, and goes through only if the shover is strong enough for the line's total weight. So a piece standing alone is light and easy to throw, while the same piece with a friend lined up behind it is too heavy to move, and every turn asks whether to stack or to strike. The bulls are the only pieces that can move a real weight, but a bull sent out to shove is a bull no longer bracing anyone, and a lone bull is itself just light enough for an enemy bull to throw. The stones are pure ballast: heavy, slow and unable to shove, they make a line safe and do nothing else. The darts are quick and light, able to run two cells and knock a lone dart off the edge, and are the first pieces to be lost when they stray. Because every cell has three lines through it, a group braced against a shove from one side is usually light along another. Each turn is two moves, which lets a player step up and shove in the same turn, or shove and then brace the piece that shoved; the first player's single opening move keeps the start even. Both armies begin on their own rim, the most dangerous place on the board, so a game opens with a scramble off the edge and into the middle, settles into a pushing match in the centre where lines lean on each other, and ends when one side has lost four pieces over the rim, or, if the shoving locks up, when a clock awards the game to whoever holds more of the seven middle cells.
